title: Foods Highest in Iron: What Actually Provides the Most

seo.title: Foods Highest in Iron: Ranking and Absorption
seo.meta_description: Oysters, liver, beans, tofu and seeds can all provide substantial iron, but heme and nonheme iron are absorbed differently.
seo.search_intent: Compare iron-rich foods using realistic servings and explain why absorption differs between animal and plant sources.

excerpt: Oysters and liver stand out among animal foods, while beans, tofu, seeds and fortified foods can also provide substantial iron. The useful comparison is not just milligrams on a chart: serving size and the difference between heme and nonheme iron matter too.
content_html:
Calling a food ‘high in iron’ sounds simple until you compare oysters, a bowl of beans and a spoonful of seeds. Iron per 100 grams can rank foods, but it does not tell you how much iron lands on a normal plate or how much your body can absorb.

The most useful sources combine a meaningful amount per serving with favorable absorption. Animal foods can provide heme iron, which is generally absorbed more efficiently. Plant foods provide nonheme iron, whose absorption is more affected by the rest of the meal.

A practical serving-level comparison

The following amounts use common prepared or ready-to-eat servings.

FoodServingIron, approx.
Cooked oysters3 oz8 mg
White beans1 cup8 mg
Cooked beef liver3 oz5 mg
Cooked lentils½ cup3 mg
Firm tofu½ cup3 mg
Cooked spinach½ cup3 mg
Cooked lean beef3 oz2 mg

The table shows why there is no single winner that answers every question. A cup of white beans can match a serving of oysters in total iron, yet the type of iron and the food matrix are very different.

Heme iron is absorbed more efficiently

Meat, organ meats, fish and shellfish provide heme iron. Its absorption is generally higher and less affected by other components of a meal. That means a moderate number of milligrams can still be nutritionally significant.

For example, a 3-ounce serving of beef may provide about 2 mg of iron, less than the roughly 3 mg in half a cup of lentils, but a larger share of the beef's iron is in the heme form.

Plant foods can provide plenty, but the meal matters

Beans, tofu, seeds, nuts and leafy greens provide nonheme iron. Vitamin C can improve its absorption, so lentils with bell pepper, tomatoes or a vitamin-C-rich fruit create a more favorable meal than lentils alone.

Phytates and some polyphenols can reduce absorption in a particular meal. That does not make beans a poor iron source; it explains why the whole dietary pattern matters more than the laboratory number alone.

Spinach contains iron, but it is not the perfect reference food

Half a cup of cooked spinach provides about 3 mg of iron, which is meaningful. However, spinach also contains compounds that limit mineral absorption. More iron on a chart therefore does not automatically mean more iron absorbed.

Seeds look especially high because they contain little water

Sesame and pumpkin seeds can show impressive iron values per 100 grams, but a normal serving is closer to 1 ounce. About 1 ounce of pumpkin seeds provides roughly 2–3 mg of iron—useful, but very different from treating 100 grams as a routine snack.

Fortified foods can completely change the ranking

Some breakfast cereals contain added iron and may provide 8, 12 or even 18 mg in one serving depending on the product. Because that iron is added, the label matters more than a generic value for ‘cereal.’

The useful rule

If you want to increase iron intake, you do not need one magic food. Use heme-rich animal foods if they fit your diet, or make plant sources such as beans, tofu and seeds regular foods and pair them with vitamin C. Total intake and absorption matter as much as a ranking position.

faq.question: What food is highest in iron?
faq.answer: Oysters, liver and some fortified foods are among the most concentrated sources. Beans, tofu and seeds are strong plant sources, though their nonheme iron is absorbed differently.

faq.question: Do lentils have more iron than beef?
faq.answer: They can provide a similar or higher amount of total iron per serving, but beef contains heme iron, which is generally absorbed more efficiently.

faq.question: Does vitamin C help iron absorption?
faq.answer: Yes. Vitamin C can improve absorption of nonheme iron from beans, tofu, grains and vegetables.
